newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine January inflation contained at 5.0 pct.
newsitem.headline: Philippine January inflation contained at 5.0 pct.

text.p: Keen competition and abundant food supplies in local markets contained Philippine inflation to an annualised 5.0 percent in January, down from 5.2 percent in December last year, economists said on Wednesday.
The month-on-month inflation rate slowed down to 0.6 percent in January from 0.8 percent the previous month, the National Statistics Office (NSO) earlier announced.
Sub-indices of the food, beverages and tobacco, services, and fuel, light and water sectors registered lower rates in January, pulling down the overall inflation rate, the NSO said.

"It's the stable food prices that brought down the inflation ... The supply is so plentiful that it will more than offset any increase in oil prices," said Luz Lorenzo, chief economist at Peregrine Securities.
She said good harvests last year boosted supply in the market, warding off inflationary pressures from successive increases in domestic petrol prices.

Earlier, analysts had anticipated a slight rise in January inflation after oil companies raised petroleum prices in January, following two increases in December and an announcement of a new round of wage hikes late last month.
A Reuters survey of six investment houses last week showed analysts were expecting January inflation to average at an annualised 5.36 percent.

Socioeconomic Planning Secretary Cielito Habito, in a report to President Fidel Ramos, said the government maintained its 6.0 to 6.5 percent average inflation target for the year despite the oil price and wage hikes.
Without the wage and oil price adjustments, the full year average would have been at 5.2 percent this year, Habito said. The country's average inflation last year was at 8.4 percent.
Arnold Oliva, an economist at PCIB Securities, said keener competition among food manufacturers also kept prices from spiralling upward.
"The market is very, very competitive. Traders would rather absorb the increasing costs at this time," Oliva said.
DBS Securities economist Al Rillo said the steady and generally low inflation in the past few months had changed the public consumption pattern.

"Price distortion is no longer prevalent. People do not hoard at the slightest sign of a pending price hike," he said. Annual inflation dipped within single digits through the second half of 1996 after double-digit rises in the first half.
NSO administrator Tomas Africa said a deregulated environment had also kept traders from speculating and manipulating prices. In 1995, rice traders hoarded stocks, pushing domestic prices skyward.
As for the wage increase which would take effect in February, Rillo said surplus labour would absorb any significant rise in production costs.
But PCIB Securities' Oliva said he still foresaw the inflation rate edging up in coming months because producers would adjust their prices once they could no longer endure the rising costs.

Maria Theresa Aclo, a research associate at the Bankers Association of the Philippines' policy research group, also said an inflation uptrend was possible in the second half of the year as the effects of election spending trickled in.
The country is scheduled to hold presidential and national elections in May next year.
